name: libucl
workload: Parse and emit a 19 MB JSON file of about 700 thousand lines generated with json-generator.com, timing the whole-file parse and each emit format.
claimed_speedup: Parse: jansson 1.3899 s vs UCL 0.6649 s (about 2.1x, derived from page data); UCL built with -O3 parses in 0.3002 s (about 4.6x vs the jansson figure, derived from page data, but the jansson figure is not stated to be -O3). Emit: jansson 0.2609 s vs UCL config 0.2423 s, JSON 0.2329 s, compact JSON 0.1811 s, YAML 0.2489 s (about 1.1x for JSON, derived from page data); UCL -O3 emit 0.1174 s config and JSON, 0.0991 s compact JSON, 0.1354 s YAML.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the jansson run. The first UCL set is described only as unoptimized, the second as 'compiled with optimizations (-O3)'.
tradeoffs: UCL is a configuration language that is a superset of JSON (macros, includes, variables, comments, implicit arrays, multiple values per key, JSON Schema v4 validation) with CBOR and MessagePack input and output, so the parse does more than plain JSON. The README warns that with all features enabled it is meant for trusted configuration input only and must not take adversarial input. C API with an object tree; zero-copy parsing is an opt-in flag (UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY). Bindings for Lua, Python and Haskell live in the repo.
caveats: First-party README numbers from one run on one generated file: no CPU, OS, compiler version, jansson version or jansson build flags are given, and the two UCL sets differ in optimization level, so the unoptimized and -O3 ratios mix builds. tests/test_speed.c in the repo times only UCL (it mmaps the file and uses UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY); the jansson harness is not in the repo, so the comparison is not reproducible from public code. The README does not say whether the quoted run used the zero-copy flag, which would favour UCL over jansson (which allocates its own strings). The emit gap against jansson is small. The benchmark harness source carries a 2013 copyright header, so the numbers are probably old. No independent benchmark including libucl was found.

name: PicoHTTPParser
workload: Parse one HTTP/1.1 GET request (9 headers including a Cookie, 430 bytes) 100000 times in a loop, headers not inspected, single thread, timing with clock().
claimed_speedup: 100000 request parses: picohttpparser 0.036571 s vs http-parser 0.289766 s, about 7.9x (derived from page data); the same page puts fast-http (Common Lisp) at 0.138 s and says picohttpparser is '3.7 times faster' than fast-http.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O3 for both bench.c programs; environment listed as 'GCC version 6.0 (clang-600.0.51)' (Apple clang on OS X). http_parser.o is produced by 'make' in the http-parser repo, whose current Makefile builds http_parser.o with -O3 (the 2014 Makefile was not checked).
hardware: MacBook Pro, OS X Mavericks, 3GHz Intel Core i7, 8GB RAM (exact CPU model not given)
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; HTTP/1 parser of H2O; used by Perl modules Plack, Starman, Starlet and Furl
tradeoffs: Stateless one-shot parser over a complete buffer: it allocates nothing and returns pointers into the caller's buffer, so the caller re-calls with the whole buffer after partial reads (prevbuflen hint) and no callbacks are offered. Also provides phr_parse_response, phr_parse_headers and phr_decode_chunked. http-parser is a streaming callback-driven state machine, so the two do not do identical work.
caveats: Independent measurement taken by the author of the fast-http Common Lisp parser (the page is a copy of the fukamachi/fast-http README at an older commit, and its note says an earlier chart was deleted 'because the benchmark was wrong'; the current upstream README no longer carries the picohttpparser rows). A microbenchmark of one request repeated 100000 times (about 37 ms for picohttpparser), clock() with float timestamps, 2014 hardware and compilers, single run. The http-parser run used null callbacks. The README command line for the picohttpparser run shows 'gcc ... http_parser.c bench.c', which looks like a copy-paste slip. The picohttpparser README's own benchmark is a PNG chart hosted on gyazo that could not be read here; the repo's bench.c times picohttpparser alone (10 million parses) with no competitor. CPU model is generic ('3GHz Intel Core i7'), which keeps this at B rather than A.

name: simdzone
baseline: Knot DNS libzscanner (zscanner) 3.3.4, and NSD 4.9's previous zonec zone parser
workload: Complete parse of the Sweden (.se) DNS zone file, 1361515551 bytes, one thread, counting accepted resource records in a callback; the harness includes disk read (file expected in page cache).
claimed_speedup: se.zone.txt: simdzone Haswell (AVX2) kernel 0.81 GB/s vs Knot 3.3.4 0.19 GB/s, about 4.3x (derived from page data); Westmere (SSE4.2) kernel 0.73 GB/s (about 3.8x, derived); scalar fallback kernel 0.38 GB/s (about 2.0x, derived). Cycles per byte 3.38 (Haswell) vs 17.06 (Knot); instructions per byte 11.90 vs 23.45.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release (default when no build type is given), C11 and C++20; Dockerfile is ubuntu:24.04 with g++ and clang installed; simdzone pinned to commit aab6386, zonec to 0196635, Knot from the libknot-dev package. Exact compiler and flags used for the quoted run are not stated.
hardware: CPU model not stated on the pages opened; the README output shows clock readings of 2.72 GHz to 3.16 GHz from Linux perf counters. The simdzone README separately quotes an Intel Core i7-1065G7 run (clang 17.0.6, Fedora 39) with no baseline.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; replaced the zone parser in NSD (NLnet Labs authoritative name server)
tradeoffs: SIMD kernels exist only for x86-64 (SSE4.2 Westmere and AVX2 Haswell, selected at run time); RISC-V and other targets use the scalar fallback kernel (0.38 GB/s in the quoted run, still about 2x Knot). Callback-based C library, deserializer only for now (serializer planned). Parts copied from simdjson under its BSD licence.
caveats: The quoted table is from the benchmark repo of Daniel Lemire, co-author of the simdzone paper (Koekkoek and Lemire, 'Parsing Millions of DNS Records per Second', Software: Practice and Experience 2025), so it is not independent of the project, and the README example output predates the zonec (NSD 4.9) row that bench.cpp now runs. The paper itself could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked); a WebSearch snippet of it quotes simdzone above 0.8 GB/s, Knot DNS at 0.19 to 0.32 GB/s and NSD's parser at 0.05 to 0.07 GB/s (snippet only, not verified on a page). The tier stays B because the CPU model and exact compiler are not given on reachable pages. Single file (the .se zone) in the README; the benchmark counts records through callbacks rather than building a zone. The simdzone repo README states no baseline comparison of its own.
